title: AgentMercury: Synthesizing Worlds, Not Tasks
hook: Instead of building an environment per task, build a persistent business world with entities, services and invariants — and let the tasks fall out of it.
key_points: Agent RL is bottlenecked on environments, usually hand-built or synthesized around a target benchmark.
AgentMercury inverts this: instantiate a persistent world (entities, services, tools, state, executable cross-service invariants) first.
Diverse tasks and interaction trajectories then emerge from the world instead of being specified up front.
4,783 executable environments were generated across 14 industries and 50 countries as RL training substrate.
Qwen3.5-4B improved 12.3 → 15.7 on EnterpriseOps-GYM and 45.9 → 56.0 on AIME26 — gains transferring out of domain.
World construction is itself learnable: fine-tuning on construction traces lifted authoring success from 3.3% to 83.3%.
content_html: Training agents means having somewhere for them to act, and environments are expensive — usually handwritten, or generated backwards from whatever benchmark you plan to report on. Minbyul Jeong and Chanwoong Yoon argue that this task-centric framing is the bottleneck, and flip it: AgentMercury takes a high-level business scenario and instantiates a persistent world of entities, services, tools, state, and executable cross-service invariants. Tasks and trajectories then emerge from the world.
extra_html: They generate 4,783 executable environments spanning 14 industries and 50 countries and use them as reinforcement-learning substrate. Despite no benchmark targeting, the paper reports Qwen3.5-4B improving from 12.3 to 15.7 on EnterpriseOps-GYM and from 45.9 to 56.0 on AIME26, along with gains on coding, scientific computing and tool use. A second result is arguably the more useful one: fine-tuning Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on construction traces raised executable-world authoring success from 3.3% to 83.3% on held-out scenarios — the environment factory can be learned too. Paper on arXiv.

related.title: Agentic Environment Engineering: A Survey
related.hook: Agents only get as good as the worlds they practice in. This survey maps the full lifecycle of agent environments — how we model, synthesize, evaluate, and grow them.

related.title: Skill Self-Play: Pushing the Frontier of LLM Capability with Co-Evolving Skills
related.hook: Self-evolving models face a dilemma: verifiable environments are narrow, open-ended task generation is unreliable. This uses agent skills as the middle ground.

flashcards.prompt: What distinguishes AgentMercury's approach from typical environment synthesis?

choices.text: It instantiates a persistent world with state and invariants first, then lets tasks emerge from it
It generates one hand-verified environment per benchmark task
It replaces environments entirely with a reward model

flashcards.explanation_html: The paper calls the usual approach 'task-centric' and argues it can't scale to realistic evolving workflows; building the world first lets diverse tasks emerge naturally.

flashcards.prompt: Why is it significant that AIME26 scores improved after training on business environments?
flashcards.back_html: The environments were built without targeting that benchmark, so the gain suggests scenario-grounded environments give learning signal that generalizes out of domain — into reasoning, coding, and tool use.

flashcards.prompt: What did the authors show about the environment-construction process itself?
flashcards.back_html: It is a learnable capability. Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on construction traces raised executable-world authoring success on held-out scenarios from 3.3% to 83.3%.
